source: Casasanto (2010) Space for Thinking: Experiments 1-5, space and time interference
finding: English speakers who see a line grow on screen judge its duration by its length. Duration does not bias length judgements. Space drives time, not the reverse, as in metaphor.
numbers: Exp 1: 162 lines (200-800 px, 50 px steps) shown 1-5 s in 500 ms steps; space affected time estimates, duration did not affect space estimates. Accuracy equal in both domains. Exps 2-5 ruled out task-demand and memory explanations.
limits: Chapter summarising the lab's own studies. English only here, so this shows an asymmetry, not a language effect.
agent_relevance: Time words are borrowed from space words in training text, so an asymmetry in how a model mixes distance into duration is expected.

source: Casasanto (2010) Space for Thinking: Experiments 7-9, English vs Greek
finding: English uses distance metaphors for time (long time), Greek uses amount metaphors (much time). Nonlinguistic tasks matched this: English speakers were swayed by line length, Greek speakers by how full a tank was.
numbers: Corpus (Exp 7): long-time phrases more frequent in English and French, much-time in Greek and Spanish. Exps 8-9: Language x Task interaction F(1,56)=10.41, p=.002, no main effects. Upward-growing-line control showed no language difference, so orientation was not the cause.
limits: Total N about 60 (about 30 per language). Two languages, no preregistration, no independent replication found this session. Greek and English groups may differ in culture.
agent_relevance: Best case for a language effect that survives non-verbal responses. Per-language wording of duration may shift an LLM's estimates.

source: Casasanto (2010) Space for Thinking: Experiment 10, metaphor training
finding: About 30 minutes of using amount words (more/less) to compare durations made English speakers behave like Greek speakers on the nonlinguistic filling-tank task.
numbers: 192 fill-in-the-blank sentences. Slope of tank-fullness effect on time greater after amount training than distance training: difference 0.89, t(28)=1.73, p<.05. N about 30 total.
limits: Weak significance (t=1.73), small N, described as transient. No retention test.
agent_relevance: Priming wording changes a later judgement briefly. Prompt phrasing effects are probably short-lived and local.

source: Dolscheid, Shayan, Majid, Casasanto (2011) The Thickness of Musical Pitch, CogSci proceedings, Exp 1
finding: Dutch speakers (height words for pitch) had sung pitches pulled by irrelevant line height. Farsi speakers (thick/thin words) were pulled by irrelevant line thickness. Interference followed the native metaphor.
numbers: N=40 Dutch, N=40 Farsi (20 per task). Language x Task F(1,79)=10.73, p=.002. Dutch height > Farsi height t(38)=2.65, p=.01. Farsi thickness > Dutch thickness t(38)=2.00, p=.05. Controlling music-reading ability: F(1,79)=10.83, p=.002. Within-domain accuracy did not interact (F=0.45).
limits: Farsi speakers recruited in the Netherlands (Nijmegen, Delft), so bilingual and acculturated. Farsi pitch accuracy lower (slopes about .6 vs .9-1.0). Some single-group tests marginal (Farsi thickness p=.05).
agent_relevance: Native metaphor choice predicts a non-verbal mapping. A model trained on Dutch vs Farsi text could in principle inherit such mappings.

source: Dolscheid et al. (2011) Exp 2, thickness training of Dutch speakers
finding: 20 minutes of filling in blanks with thinner/thicker (Farsi-like) made Dutch speakers show a thickness-on-pitch effect like native Farsi speakers. Height training did not.
numbers: N=60 (30 per group). Training accuracy 99% in both. Thickness slope 1.46 (p=.003) after thickness training vs 0.08 (ns) after height training; difference 1.38, t(58)=1.84, p=.07 two-tailed. Not different from Farsi natives, t(48)=1.12 ns; larger than untrained Dutch, t(48)=2.02, p=.05.
limits: The key contrast between trained groups is p=.07, not significant at .05. Support comes mostly from comparing to other groups. Conference version.
agent_relevance: Short language practice may shift a non-verbal mapping, but the evidence is borderline. Do not build scaffold rules on it.

source: Dolscheid et al. (2013) The thickness of musical pitch, Psychological Science 24:613-621
finding: Journal version of the Dutch-Farsi pitch study with the same design: pitch reproduction with irrelevant height or thickness, plus Dutch training.
numbers: Not opened in full. Abstract and conference version (b04, b05) were read. Abstract says Dutch speakers after training resembled Farsi speakers.
limits: Full text not fetched (paywalled). Numbers in the journal version may differ from the conference version.
agent_relevance: Cite via the conference numbers only.

source: Dolscheid, Hunnius, Casasanto, Majid (2020) Space-pitch associations differ in their susceptibility to language, Cognition
finding: Dutch and Turkish speakers both link thickness to pitch in simple association tasks, so the thickness-pitch link is not created by language. The height-pitch link differs by language.
numbers: Thickness-pitch above chance in both groups (Dutch M=95%, d=2.58). Language x Task chi2(1)=67.73, p<.001; height-pitch differs by language (chi2(1)=54.72, p<.001) but thickness-pitch does not (chi2(1)=.91, p=.34). N=40 per group.
limits: Association tasks differ from the 2013 interference tasks, so this is not a direct replication. Turkish group read music better (d=.74), controlled statistically. Author list in this note is partial.
agent_relevance: Narrows the claim: some mappings are universal, only some are malleable by language.

source: Dolscheid et al. (2020) conflict task: thick-high vs thin-low pitched against each other
finding: When a thick line high in space competes with a thin line low, Turkish speakers pick thickness for pitch and Dutch speakers split about evenly.
numbers: Turkish height-pitch choice M=15%, t(39)=-9.71, p<.001, d=-1.54 (thickness preferred). Dutch M=50%, t(39)=.06, p=.95. Excluding 5 Dutch and 1 Turkish without a clear strategy: 36 of 39 Turkish (92%) chose thickness; Dutch 17 of 35 (49%) height, 18 of 35 (51%) thickness.
limits: Dutch speakers split into two strategy groups, so the language effect is not uniform within a group. Turkish speakers rather than Farsi, so a different language from 2013.
agent_relevance: Per-person variation is large and averages hide it. Single-answer prompts hide the same spread in LLM outputs.

source: Boroditsky (2001) Does language shape thought? Mandarin and English speakers' conceptions of time (as described by later papers)
finding: English speakers were faster to confirm time statements after a horizontal spatial prime, Mandarin speakers after a vertical prime. Training English speakers to say March is above April made them look like Mandarin speakers.
numbers: Original statistics not read. Described in Chen et al. (2011) and Casasanto (2010), which give no sample sizes.
limits: Failed to replicate in Chen 2007, January & Kako 2007, Tse & Altarriba 2008, Sanvido et al. 2011 (list from Chen et al. 2011, b10). Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Famous result that did not hold: a warning against building agent rules on one priming study.

source: Chen, Liang, O'Seaghdha, Huang (2011) English and Mandarin speakers may think about time differently, but for a different reason
finding: Repeating the Boroditsky, Fuhrman, McCormick task: Taiwan Mandarin speakers showed the opposite pattern to English speakers, but mainland China Mandarin speakers resembled English speakers. Writing direction, not metaphor, fits better.
numbers: Three failed replications of the 2001 priming result listed: Chen 2007, January & Kako 2007, Tse & Altarriba 2008. Samples: US English, Taiwan Mandarin, China Mandarin; exact N not on the abstract page.
quote: the claim did not stand in three failed replications
limits: Only the abstract page was available. Quasi-experimental: Taiwan vs China differ in more than text direction.
agent_relevance: A rival explanation (orthography) can explain a seeming language effect. Check confounds before attributing a model behaviour to language.

source: Chen, Friederich, Shu (2017) Whether Chinese speakers think about time more vertically depends on reading experience: contextual priming
finding: Holding language constant (Mandarin), reading vertical text just before a time task created a vertical bias in Taiwan readers and removed it after horizontal text. China readers showed no vertical bias, and a horizontal bias after vertical text.
numbers: 56 Taiwan and 56 China participants. Taiwan: overall STARC effect F(1,7915)=59.18; vertical > horizontal key orientation F(1,7915)=11.13, p=.0009; under vertical prime orientation x canonicity F(1,3952)=18.51, p<.0001; under horizontal prime F(1,3927)=.35, p=.56.
limits: Trial-level mixed models with large df; only 56 people per site. Reading experience is self-report. Page year printed as 2017.
agent_relevance: Context just before a task can override a supposed language effect. In prompts, preceding text may matter more than the language.

source: Chen et al. (2017) discussion: reading experience explains vertical time bias better than metaphor
finding: The authors conclude that orthographic direction and lifetime plus immediate reading experience explain vertical bias, not use of vertical spatial metaphors.
numbers: China questionnaire (1-7 scale): vertical text experience 2.7 (SD 1.6), horizontal left-to-right 6.9 (SD .7). China STARC error rate 3%.
limits: Self-reported experience; priming then test in one session.
agent_relevance: A discriminating design: hold language fixed, vary reading input. For an LLM: hold language fixed, vary context.

source: Yang, Gu, Fang, Sun (2022) Mental representations of time in English monolinguals, Mandarin monolinguals and Mandarin-English bilinguals, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: With a mouse-placement temporal congruency task, Mandarin monolinguals showed a sagittal and a vertical (top=earlier) advantage; English monolinguals only the sagittal. The language difference was in the vertical axis.
numbers: Exp 1: 91 valid participants (df=89; 51 Mandarin, 40 English). Language x Axis x Directionality F1(1,89)=7.83, p=.006, eta_p2=.081. Vertical: Language x Direction F1(1,89)=12.58, eta_p2=.124; Mandarin top-earlier faster t(50)=-5.76, d=.806; English t(39)=.98, p=.33. Sagittal advantage in both (English d=.784, Mandarin d=1.42).
limits: Languages differ in country, schooling and script habits, all confounded. Participants from China (horizontal text) yet vertical bias found, unlike Chen 2011; tasks differ (mice vs keys).
agent_relevance: A replication of the vertical difference with another paradigm: the effect exists for some tasks only.

source: Yang et al. (2022) Exp 2: Mandarin-English bilinguals
finding: Learning English did not move Mandarin speakers toward English-like time thinking, at low or high L2 proficiency.
numbers: Three groups: Mandarin monolinguals, low and high English proficiency bilinguals. Proficiency x Axis x Direction interaction F<1 (df 1,92); proficiency main effect F1(2,92)=11.69, eta_p2=.203. All groups: front-earlier faster, top-earlier faster.
limits: Age of acquisition and L2 use not controlled. F<1 is not an equivalence test.
agent_relevance: Habitual L1 patterns resist later language exposure, which conflicts with the quick-retraining story from lab training studies.

source: Crossley & Bylund (2025) Direction of reading, not writing, shapes concepts of time, Language and Cognition 17:e49
finding: Mirror-reading text made adults place the past on the right (replicating Casasanto & Bottini 2014). Mirror-writing did not, even after 5 days of training.
numbers: Reading baseline N=64: standard 87.5% past-left vs mirror 53.1% past-left; chi2=9.06, p=.003, OR=6.18, BF10=25.58. Replication N=64: 78.1% vs 40.6%, chi2=9.33, p=.002, BF10=30.71. Writing experiments (n=64 each): BF10=.23 and .24 (null); Exp 3, 5 days training: 23% vs 25.8%, chi2=.09, p=.77. Modality contrast Q=8.54.
limits: Binary mapping task, South African students, one paradigm. A cultural-practice effect, not a language-structure effect.
agent_relevance: Replicated with Bayes factors and a clean null: only some habits shape thought. A model for how a well-powered test looks.

source: Casasanto & Bottini (2014) Mirror reading can reverse the flow of time, J Exp Psychol Gen 143:473-479 (as summarised in Crossley & Bylund 2025)
finding: Dutch speakers randomly assigned to read mirror-reversed text mapped time right-to-left in space-time congruity tasks. Rotated text rotated the mapping.
numbers: Original statistics not read; replication numbers in b15.
limits: Original not opened (download failed). Support here is from the 2025 replication.
agent_relevance: Short reading practice flips a spatial time mapping: context-induced mappings are cheap to change.

source: Martinovic, Paramei, MacInnes (2020) Russian blues reveal the limits of language influencing colour discrimination, Cognition
finding: Using the same tasks as Winawer et al. 2007, Russian speakers showed no faster discrimination across the sinij/goluboj boundary than within it.
numbers: Exp 1: N=18 Russian, N=20 English recruited. Best mixed model had no boundary effect (chi2(1)=1.10, p=.29) and no boundary x language interaction (chi2(1)=1.19, p=.28). English controls faster overall by 112 ms (SE 48; chi2(1)=5.04, p=.025).
limits: Small samples. Colour is not a time, space or pitch domain.
agent_relevance: A flagship Whorfian psychophysics effect failed a close replication; do not assume lab effects transfer.

source: Martinovic et al. (2020) Exp 2: boundary shifts with stimulus frequency
finding: In categorisation, the sinij/goluboj boundary moved toward lighter shades in a light-biased context. The English dark blue/light blue boundary did not move. Authors say the Russian boundary is less well-structured than claimed.
numbers: Three frequency contexts (unbiased, more sinij, more goluboj). Frequency bias shifted only the Russian boundary. Trial-to-trial (N-1) effects present.
limits: Small N. Categorisation, not discrimination.
agent_relevance: Category edges set by language shift with the examples seen. In a model, examples shown in a prompt can move category edges.

source: Winawer et al. (2007) Russian blues reveal effects of language on colour discrimination, PNAS (as described by later papers)
finding: Russian speakers discriminated dark and light blues faster across the sinij/goluboj boundary. The advantage was said to vanish under verbal interference.
numbers: Original numbers not read. Martinovic et al. 2020 note the original no-interference baseline was about 180 ms.
limits: Not opened. The verbal-interference result is the main evidence that language acts online.
agent_relevance: Interference points to language acting at the moment of judgement, which an LLM always has.

source: Cibelli, Xu, Austerweil, Griffiths, Regier (2016) The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis and probabilistic inference: evidence from the domain of color, PLoS ONE 11:e0158725
finding: A Bayesian model with a universal perceptual space plus language-specific categories predicts that category effects are largest when perceptual memory is uncertain. It fits English colour-memory bias and cross-language discrimination data, and explains why some effects do not replicate.
numbers: Abstract-level read only: model fits to existing datasets, no new human sample.
quote: categories will most clearly affect color memory when perceptual information is uncertain
limits: Fitted to earlier data, not a preregistered test. Colour only.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb: language matters most when evidence is noisy. For an LLM, wording may matter most when a question is ambiguous or underspecified.

source: Casasanto (2010) framing: Shallow View vs Deep View of language-thought links
finding: Under the Shallow View, language affects thought only while speaking. Under the Deep View, long-term experience with metaphors reshapes non-verbal mappings. Non-verbal psychophysical tasks are the discriminating test.
numbers: No new numbers. Predicts no cross-language difference in nonlinguistic tasks under the Shallow View and a difference matching metaphor use under the Deep View.
limits: Written 2010, before the failed replications (b10) and the 2020 pitch results, and by an advocate of the Deep View.
agent_relevance: Every LLM output is verbal, so only Shallow-view (online wording) effects can be tested in LLMs directly.

source: Under the Shadow of Babel (Wang et al. 2025) BICAUSE bilingual causal reasoning, Findings of EMNLP
finding: Qwen1.5-1.8B-Chat is equally accurate on forward English and Chinese causal chains but degrades more on reversed Chinese chains. The authors read this as the model internalising language-specific causal order habits.
numbers: Forward chain accuracy: English 91.0%, Chinese 91.2%. Reversed: English 88.5%, Chinese 76.5%. SVCCA similarity of attention: EN vs ZH forward 0.73; EN forward vs reversed 0.64; ZH forward vs reversed about 0.46.
limits: One small model for the main numbers. Appendix: Llama-3.2-1B En 61.0 vs Zh 49.8 average, Llama-3.2-3B En 27.0. Chinese reversed chains may simply be rarer in training data (frequency, not cognition). No human control.
agent_relevance: Order bias in a model, not a proven Whorfian effect. Test reversed or unusual orderings in agent prompts and see if it breaks.

source: Zhang & Rayz (2026) Structured yet bounded temporal understanding in LLMs, arXiv 2510.16685v2
finding: LLMs adapt to two temporal frames of reference (deictic past-present-future vs sequential before-after) with different similarity structures: graded and asymmetric around now under deictic, strongly negative between separated events under sequential.
numbers: Wikidata events with similarity judgement scores. Deictic frame: sharper decline for future than past, higher variance in the past, duration affected only past events. No effect sizes extracted from the abstract and introduction I read.
limits: Not a Whorfian test: no human comparison and no cross-language manipulation. Cites Gentner, Imai and Boroditsky (2002) for space-time metaphor framing only.
agent_relevance: How a time question is framed changes how a model scores event similarity. State the temporal frame explicitly in prompts.

source: Pan et al. (2026) Do LLMs build world models from text? MENTALMAP multilingual diagnostic of spatial reasoning, arXiv 2605.28277
finding: Across eight languages and 13 LLMs, pure-text spatial reasoning collapses at viewpoint-taking (L3) in every language. Humans doing the same text task also score 0% at L3.
numbers: 1,950 evaluation cells. L3 under half of L0 in every (model, language) cell in the diagnostic regime. Human pilot: L3=0% in all eight languages, L4 about 41% (std 3.3 pp). Script-family L3 means: Latin 14.8, CJK 16.8, Arabic 11.4; Arabic gap vs English -24.7 pp. CoT: +32 pp DeepSeek-V4-Flash, -16 pp Qwen2.5-7B at L3.
limits: Language differences found are performance gaps (Latin vs CJK vs Arabic/Thai), not shown to be relativity. The authors read the cliff as a working-memory limit of text. Human pilot is about 3 people per language.
agent_relevance: Argues against a language-specific cause for the big spatial failure: it is the text modality. Add a scratchpad for viewpoint changes rather than switching language.

source: Vision-language model as a Whorfian subject (Cognitive Science Society paper found via search; not opened)
finding: A search summary says a language-conditioned colour boundary shift appears in a vision-language model only when visual representations are aligned with language, not in vision-only embeddings.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only a search snippet; PDF download failed. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, language effects need the language-aligned layer, a clue where to look for Whorfian effects in models.

source: Chen (2007), January & Kako (2007), Tse & Altarriba (2008): failed replications of Boroditsky 2001
finding: Three independent labs could not reproduce the Mandarin-vertical priming difference. Chen also reports Mandarin uses horizontal time metaphors more than vertical ones.
numbers: Chen reports four failed attempts (per a search-result abstract). No sample sizes read.
limits: Known only via secondary text (Chen et al. 2011, search abstracts). Originals not opened.
agent_relevance: A core Whorfian time finding had three failed replications. Treat as not robust.

source: Boroditsky, Fuhrman, McCormick (2011) Do English and Mandarin speakers think about time differently? Cognition
finding: Authors argue Mandarin speakers use vertical representations of time more than English speakers in new tasks. Later work (Chen et al. 2017, b11) found this depends on Taiwan vs China reading habits.
numbers: Not read. Per Chen et al. 2017: Chen and O'Seaghdha observed a vertical bias in Taiwan Mandarin but not China Mandarin.
limits: Only the search listing and secondary accounts.
agent_relevance: Another effect that holds in one sub-population only.

source: Dolscheid et al. (2011) discussion: notation confound and associative-learning account
finding: The authors rule out musical notation (higher notes written higher in both cultures) using music-reading ratings, and propose that each metaphor use strengthens a mapping (associative learning).
numbers: Music-reading as covariate: Language x Task F(1,79)=10.83, p=.002. Three-way Language x Task x Domain F(1,159)=6.12, p=.02. Infants of 3-4 months prefer height-pitch congruence (cited from Walker et al. 2010).
limits: Covariate is one self-rating (1-7). Infant evidence shows some pitch-space coupling is not language.
agent_relevance: The associative account predicts that phrase frequency in training data strengthens a mapping in a model, a testable hypothesis.
